title: Paddy Power cuts 1,400 jobs and blames betting tax rises
description: Paddy Power-owner Flutter has announced plans to cut up to 1,400 jobs as its boss claimed the company "cannot fully absorb" tax rises imposed on the g
body: Paddy Power-owner Flutter has announced plans to cut up to 1,400 jobs as its boss claimed the company "cannot fully absorb" tax rises imposed on the gambling industry.Staff based in Leeds and Dublin, as well as workers for its UK and Ireland business at Flutter's Portugal and Romania sites, will be most affected, but what roles are at risk has not been disclosed.The government announced taxes rises on online casino and sports betting, with an exemption for horse racing, in the Budget last year.Flutter boss Kevin Harrington said the tax hikes had "fundamentally changed" the economic model of the UK betting and gaming industry, arguing it had helped "fuel the unlicensed, unregulated market"."We continue to expect these tax increases to have a very significant impact on the overall market," Flutter Entertainment said on Tuesday.Flutter, which also owns Sky Bet and Betfair, employs 28,500 people across the world, including 9,000 in the UK and Ireland.As well as its Leeds and Dublin offices, the BBC understands the cuts could also affect staff based in London and Sunderland, as well as Malta and Gibraltar.Harrington, who is chief executive of the betting giant's UK and Ireland business, said: "As we warned a year ago, we cannot fully absorb a rise of this magnitude without reducing our fixed cost base and therefore must restructure our business so that we can best position ourselves for the future."A government spokesperson said the job cuts were a "commercial decision for Flutter, not the UK government"."However, we understand this will be a difficult time for the workers," they added.Flutter delisted from the London Stock Exchange in August in a blow to the UK, with its shares now solely traded in New York.In its most recent results, the company reported a $299m (£224m) pre-tax loss for the three months to June for its entire business worldwide, compared to a $205m profit in the same period last year. Sales rose 3% to $4.3bn.However, revenues in the UK and Ireland rose by 4% over the period, due to strong growth in online gambling games. Some online gambling tax rises announced in last year's Budget took effect in April. This included remote gaming duty, which is paid on online casino betting, rising from 21% to 40%.General betting duty, paid on the profits made from various forms of sports betting, was kept at 15% in betting shops, but is set to rise from 15% to 25% online in April next year.Betting firms had warned that cost increases would lead to job losses and betting shop closures, but MPs dismissed the warnings as "scaremongering".During the summer, Ladbrokes owner Entain announced job cuts, with news agency Reuters reporting 500 roles were being removed.Punters' winnings from gambling are not taxed in the UK, nor is VAT charged on bets.Flutter said its restructuring plan would cost between $80m and $90m.The company has claimed in previous financial results that the impact of UK tax rises would hit its underlying profit by $320m this year and $540m in 2027, before any savings or restructure to mitigate the impact.

schema.headline: Paddy Power cuts 1,400 jobs and blames betting tax rises

title: Zelensky and US envoys holding Oslo talks as Rubio denies withholding intelligence
description: US special envoy Steve Witkoff and Volodymyr Zelensky are meeting in Oslo, with relations on the slide between the Ukrainian leader and US President D
body: US special envoy Steve Witkoff and Volodymyr Zelensky are meeting in Oslo, with relations on the slide between the Ukrainian leader and US President Donald Trump.Norwegian Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Støre said Zelensky had asked Oslo and neighbouring Finland to organise the talks with the US and European allies "at a critical time for Ukraine".US Secretary of State Marco Rubio earlier rejected as "scandalous" accusations that Ukrainians were dying because the US was withholding intelligence from Kyiv.He was speaking after Zelensky's top military adviser Serhii Beskrestnov told the BBC the lack of reliable US warnings - including about ballistic missile launches - meant lives were being lost."This looks very strange," said Beskrestnov, widely known as "Flash". "Sometimes we receive this information before the attack, another time we [do] not."Relations between Kyiv and the US have soured in recent weeks to the extent that Trump has said it is time for Ukraine to get a new president, and most recently "for somebody else to negotiate on behalf of Ukraine".Zelensky first met the Norwegian prime minister and Finnish President Alexander Stubb, ahead of his talks in person with Witkoff, with Trump's son-in-law Jared Kushner taking part via video link. Støre said the aim of the talks was to steer relations towards "a more constructive path". He told reporters at the parliament in Norway that they wanted to ensure that the war ended diplomatically with a lasting and just peace.Zelensky took with him to Oslo Ukraine's intelligence chief Rustem Umerov and influential lawmaker Davyd Arakhamia, both of whom had earlier this month held talks in Miami with Witkoff and Kushner.Those talks were reportedly ended abruptly when the Ukrainian delegation was informed Trump had announced that Moscow would immediately supply more than 300,000 tons of diesel to the US and other markets, bringing to an end American sanctions on Russian diesel exports.Zelensky had reacted by calling it "a happy birthday present for Putin".Ahead of next month's US midterm elections, Trump has blamed Ukraine's attacks on Russian oil refineries for fuel prices which have reached record highs at the pump since the start of the US-led war on Iran.Speaking before the Oslo talks, Zelensky said he had had a "constructive discussion" with Rubio about the need for US early warnings, missile interceptors and SpaceX's Starlink internet network. Last week a bipartisan group of US senators called for an urgent investigation into speed restrictions to the Starlink network in Ukraine. Unconfirmed reports on Tuesday said the transfer of more Patriot interceptors - the only effective weapon in shooting down Russian ballistic missiles - had not yet been approved.Rubio is currently on a visit to India and admitted to reporters that it may be true that Patriot interceptor missiles - the only had not yet arrived in Ukraine, although nothing had been denied to Kyiv intentionally.Zelensky was set to join his Norwegian and Finnish counterparts for a press conference after the talks, but Witkoff was not expected to join them, according to the government in Oslo, external.It is not yet clear whether Witkoff will travel on to Russia after Oslo, however the Kremlin spokesman said he hoped a meeting with Trump's envoy could be organised in the near future. Dmitry Peskov said "we greatly appreciate the mediation efforts of the American negotiators".European leaders have expressed concern about recent statements from the US towards Russia, and German Chancellor Friedrich Merz spoke on Monday of "mixed pictures and messages" on the war, adding that he was trying to convince the American government "in total that this is something we have to resolve jointly". He pointed out that the US had not been paying for the defence of Ukraine since the start of 2025, and Europe and other countries were shouldering the burden."It's really a big effort for our budgets, it's really a big thing for the European Union, but we are doing that and we are trying to keep on doing that until this terrible war ends," the German leader told Bloomberg TV.Asked whether or not Ukraine was a US ally, Vice-President JD Vance has said in a TV interview that Kyiv was "certainly a partner in some ways, but we have some divergent interests from time to time, like for example... I think they should stop bombing Russian energy". "We don't have a formal alliance as far as I know with Ukraine. They're not in Nato, I don't think they should be in Nato... we're gonna work together on some things, but also we're going to be opposite on some things too."Putin launched a full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022.

schema.headline: Zelensky and US envoys holding Oslo talks as Rubio denies withholding intelligence

title: Covid failings in care homes: What the inquiry says
description: Image source, Getty ImagesByHealth correspondentThe sixth report of the Covid inquiry is highly critical of the way the government tried to protect pe
body: Image source, Getty ImagesByHealth correspondentThe sixth report of the Covid inquiry is highly critical of the way the government tried to protect people in care settings in the UK.Around 500,000 people were living in care homes at the start of the pandemic – with another million receiving care in their own homes.The inquiry said action to protect them came too late, causing devastating consequences.There were more than 43,000 recorded deaths involving Covid in care homes between March 2020 and July 2022. Here are the key findings of the 287-page report.There was no 'protective ring'At the start of the pandemic, the then-health secretary in England, Matt Hancock, said the UK government had placed "a protective ring" around care homes.But the inquiry says this was not the case, listing a catalogue of failings.It says the care sector appeared to be "something of an afterthought".A lack of personal protective equipment (PPE) meant staff had to resort to makeshift workarounds, including bin bags, festival waterproof ponchos and painters' overalls.The report is also critical of the way hospital patients who may be infected with Covid were moved to care homes to make space for others.The decision was understandable given the need to free up beds for Covid patients. But, without sufficient testing, it was important to keep these people separate and isolate them from others in case they were infected.Official guidance in March 2020 in England, Wales and Northern Ireland did not request this. That, the report says, was a significant oversight.Long-standing weaknesses undermined responseWhen the pandemic started, high levels of staff vacancies and turnover in the social care sector meant that the workforce was "fragile and lacking resilience".This undermined the ability of the sector to respond to the pandemic, the inquiry says.For example, care homes tend to rely heavily on agency staff who work in a variety of different homes. But a desire not to have staff going into multiple homes, to reduce the risk of infection transmission, meant staff shortages got even worse.Financially, care providers struggled too, as the number of people using services dropped.And for a sector that uses zero-hours contracts, there was a lack of financial support to help care staff stay off work if there was concern they might be infected.The response also suffered because of the fragmented nature of the system, with thousands of different providers and services overseen by councils. It meant the sector was more distant from government than the NHS.The pandemic, the inquiry said, exposed and exacerbated these existing weaknesses.Visiting restrictions were too tough – and caused harmThe report is clear that precautionary steps taken to restrict visiting, as part of infection control, went too far.It acknowledges there was little choice to introduce bans on visitors at the start of the pandemic, saying that was rational.But as the pandemic progressed, so did the balance between the benefits and harms of restrictions.Visits are extremely important, allowing loved ones to help residents with everything from personal care to maintaining their mental health.By September 2020, evidence suggested visitors posed a "marginal risk" – staff were judged to be the key entry point for infections.The four UK nations then started to relax their guidance, but many care homes failed to implement this and visiting remained heavily restricted.This, says the inquiry, resulted in a significant decline in the health and wellbeing of residents.Concern over blanket do not resuscitate ordersCPR (Cardiopulmonary Resuscitation), including chest compressions, can be life-saving if a person's heart has stopped beating.But doctors can sometimes opt not to resuscitate people - as can individuals themselves in advance - for example, if the individual is extremely frail or has a life-limiting illness. This should be done on an individual basis and the use of blanket do not resuscitate orders (DNACPR) is considered unlawful.The inquiry says it heard evidence of GPs imposing blanket DNACPRs on care home residents.And it pointed to records showing a sharp increase in orders being put in place – they jumped from 16,800 to 26,500 in the first nine months of the pandemic.This concern mirrors an earlier Care Quality Commission investigation which found evidence of unacceptable and inappropriate DNACPRs being put in place.The 'deep distress' of care staffThe impact on staff working in care homes was huge, affecting their mental health and wellbeing, the inquiry said.Some moved into the care homes where they worked, in an attempt to protect residents from infection. One care home owner in Wales described how 39 staff moved in for a fortnight at the start of the pandemic.Seeing so many residents die placed an enormous strain on workers, who often had to provide end-of-life care to multiple people at the same time.One care home, for example, lost half of its residents over the course of three weeks.Staff told the inquiry of the deep distress they suffered. "Staff were sitting on video calls with families, saying their last goodbye to loved ones. That was horrendous… staff were crying with the residents, because it was just so emotional for them," one said.

schema.headline: Covid failings in care homes: What the inquiry says

title: Woman describes alleged assault by Russell Brand as 'frenzied' and 'violent'
description: Warning - this report contains graphic contentA woman who claims Russell Brand sexually assaulted her has described the alleged attack as "frenzied" a
body: Warning - this report contains graphic contentA woman who claims Russell Brand sexually assaulted her has described the alleged attack as "frenzied" and "violent".Brand, 51, faces seven charges in the trial - three counts of rape, three charges of sexual assault and one of indecent assault.The allegations, made by six female complainants, span a 10-year period between 1999 and 2009. He denies the charges.On Tuesday, the jury heard from the fourth complainant in the trial, who alleges Brand sexually assaulted her at the Choice FM radio studios in central London in the mid-2000s.She said she came out of a small room in the building to find Brand outside."He said 'aye aye'," she told the jury, "he grabbed me by my face, started to kiss me, and when he was kissing me he started pushing me - his body against me."The woman continued: "He was kissing me, it was very frenzied. There was no time for me to even understand what was going on."He was running his hands over my body and I had my back against the wall at that point."From behind a blue screen, the woman described the kiss as "sloppy" and "very, very rough", when asked by the prosecution barrister about the alleged attack."His hands at the same time were all over me," she said. "He touched my bum, my breasts, his body was pressed up against me."The woman said she pushed him off and swore at him.She said there were several people with him who she claims didn't say anything about what happened after the alleged assault.The woman - now in her 50s - said she had never met Brand before and that she believed he'd been in the building because he was on Channel 4 show Big Brother's Big Mouth.She told the jury: "His whole body was pressed against me - the kisses were hard and sloppy and going down my neck. "His hands were moving so much - the reason I used the word frenzied was because it was violent. He just wasn't stopping."She said she felt "dirty" after the encounter and "never told anybody", adding: "I felt shocked and stunned, shaken."When questioned by Brand's barrister on why none of the people who may have seen what happened raised concerns, the woman said: "It was not the present-day environment.""On the day it happened - and I ask myself this question - why I didn't share it," she said. "It wasn't the culture where something happened to you and you tell people."Asked by the defence barrister why she did not go to the police, the woman said: "I would have thought about a few things. Who would have believed me?"I could lose my job and I had a mortgage to pay," she said, adding that she "buried it for so long".The woman said she came forward with the allegation after watching a documentary on television about the TV star and his alleged behaviour.Another complainant also gave evidence to the jury - again from behind a blue screen to the right side of the court.The woman who worked with Brand on a Channel 4 project in 2009, said members of the defendant's team asked her for a massage on his behalf while they were in the same space.She said after replying no, Brand "came into the room and lay his head into my lap, into my groin area".When asked by the prosecution counsel where exactly his mouth and nose were, the woman replied "in my vaginal area".The woman who worked for channel 4 at the time - said she was "so repulsed at the situation". She described him as "bony".She said she reported the alleged incident to her line manager at the time who then reported it further up the chain.Brand stared straight ahead as the complainants gave evidence - barely changing his posture. His hands sometimes resting on his lap. His wife Laura Brand remained sitting to his right side outside the dock - seeming to listen attentively to what the women were saying from the witness box.Brand denies all the charges and has pleaded not guilty.He has said that any sexual contact if it happened, would have been consensual.The trial continues.

schema.headline: Woman describes alleged assault by Russell Brand as 'frenzied' and 'violent'

title: Harry says he wants to 'reconcile' with his family
description: The Duke of Sussex has said he wants to repair his complicated relationships with his father and brother, in a magazine interview."Some people don't w
body: The Duke of Sussex has said he wants to repair his complicated relationships with his father and brother, in a magazine interview."Some people don't want it to work out. I want it to work out. With everything else that's going on in the world, the most important thing is to reconcile - that's the key point," Prince Harry told GQ in New York."Scars stick around forever. But what your perception is, and what your mindset is to those things that have happened, letting go of the past, that's something that I would encourage everybody to do," said Prince Harry.Last week Prince Harry and Meghan carried out their first public engagement together since their return to the UK in the summer.The GQ interview with Prince Harry was conducted last month and released as the Royal Family were on duty in Windsor welcoming the Sultan of Oman at the start of a state visit.But a spokesman for the Sussexes said the interview was recorded in late September and it was the entirely the publishers' decision when to run it - and that nothing should be read into the timing.The spokesman also said that the reference to "some people don't want it to work out" was not a swipe at his brother Prince William or any other member of his family.Prince Harry and Meghan moved from the UK to the United States in 2020, stepping down as working royals in what was an acrimonious departure.Harry's memoir, Spare, showed the depth of the family fall out and the damaged relationship with his brother William.Despite Prince Harry now being physically nearer to his family in the UK, there hasn't seemed to be any more emotional closeness with his brother Prince William, and in this interview Harry seems to be open to reconciliation.It was a message of wanting to build bridges that he had previously sent in a BBC interview in May 2025, when he had been living in the US.Prince Harry recognised that this royal story of family disagreements fascinated the public, saying it was "massively relatable"."Sibling disagreements, broken relationships between kids and their parents, kids and one parent - that continues to come up with me the whole time with people that I speak to," he said.Asked by GQ about the reason for his move back to the UK, Prince Harry said: "Opportunities for the family. Being able to put the kids in a British school has meant a lot to me. I didn't know how important it was to me.""They [Archie and Lilibet] are loving it, and it's just giving them a whole different experience."He told the magazine: "To be back, closer to my family, and to be back on UK soil for longer than a few days or a week here or there".Prince Harry also reflects on the King's health, following his treatment for cancer, saying: "He's getting better".There were also comments about growing up with a sense of loss after the death of his mother, Diana, Princess of Wales, in 1997."I love the fact that I'm able to now sort of carry the memory of my mother with me, with my work, rather than it hold me down, pull me back, or wallowing in that grief," he said.He rejected any sense of wanting public sympathy."I certainly don't want any sympathy. That's where we're way past that. Why? Because I'm a prince. I've got a support network around me, I've done different forms of therapy, and I put in the work. I wonder where I would be if I didn't - it could be a very different situation," he said.

schema.headline: Harry says he wants to 'reconcile' with his family

title: Man charged with attack on Australian MP as suspect's father says she is family friend
description: Image source, AFP via Getty ImagesImage caption, The community in Wangaratta remains in shock after the alleged attackByKaty WatsonAustralia correspon
body: Image source, AFP via Getty ImagesImage caption, The community in Wangaratta remains in shock after the alleged attackByKaty WatsonAustralia correspondentReporting fromWangaratta, north-east Victoria and Phelan ChatterjeeA 43-year-old man has been charged after Australian MP Helen Haines was hit by a car in the state of Victoria on Monday.The suspect will appear in court on Wednesday to face charges of dangerous driving causing serious injury, intentionally causing serious injury and the federal offence of causing harm to a public official.Local media earlier named the alleged attacker as environmental activist Brendan Nugent. His father and his partner said they had been friends with Haines "for more than 20 years" and thanked residents and officers who helped her after the "shocking and horrific crime". Haines remains in a critical condition after surgery and is reported to have lost one of her legs."Helen Haines is a deeply respected, valued and much loved member of our local community," Rod Nugent and his partner Christine Cunningham said in a statement."All of our love and all of our thoughts are with Helen and her family and friends."They promised to assist Victoria Police "in any way we can".Police say they will allege the incident was targeted.Haines, 65, the independent member for Indi, is in a critical but stable condition after undergoing surgery at a Melbourne hospital.Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Helen Haines sits as an independent MP for the electoral division of Indi in Australia's state of VictoriaShe was airlifted there after bystanders rushed to help.A local barber who was there says he pulled the suspect out of his car."I don't think I'm a hero. I think that I was just a person who had an opportunity to intervene in a safe-ish way," said Ricky Jefferies.Others who helped "didn't even check for danger", he added. "The car was still on and they sat in front of a rolling car, that's not an exaggeration."In their statement, Victoria Police say a highway patrol unit was nearby at the time of the incident and "on scene" within eight seconds of the call coming through.As they announced the charges against the 43-year-old, they said they had searched a property in Tarrawingee, around 12km (7.5 miles) from Wangaratta."At this stage it appears this is an isolated incident, and there are currently no other known threats connected to this matter," they said, adding officers would maintain a presence in Wangaratta.Haines won the seat of Indi as an independent in 2019, and has since become a prominent member of the crossbench, building rapport across Australia's increasingly divided political spectrum.The community, and country, remain in shock.At a vigil on Tuesday, locals queued patiently in the aisle of the Holy Trinity Cathedral, waiting for their turn to light a candle. Priests hugged some of those who came to pay their respects.Wangaratta's main street, where Haines's office is located, had reopened to traffic. Cars slowly filed past the growing number of bouquets being left for her on the pavement.One card read: "May you recover quickly and continue to be a light in this world."

schema.headline: Man charged with attack on Australian MP as suspect's father says she is family friend

title: Royals roll out the red carpet in Windsor for visiting Sultan
description: Tuesday evening will see Burnham's first state banquet since becoming prime minister. He will take one of the places of honour in St George's Hall, on
body: Tuesday evening will see Burnham's first state banquet since becoming prime minister. He will take one of the places of honour in St George's Hall, on a lavishly decorated table that can seat about 160 guests.Burnham previously spoke to the Sultan in July, when they discussed efforts to open the Strait of Hormuz to shipping, and the prime minister said he was grateful for Oman's attempts at mediation.The guest list does not include non-working royals, like the Duke and Duchess of Sussex.An interview with Prince Harry with GQ was released as the state visit was getting under way.He talked about his complicated relationship with his father and brother - recognising that it was something that was "massively relatable" for the public."Some people don't want it to work out," he said. "I want it to work out. "With everything else that's going on in the world, the most important thing is to reconcile - that's the key point... scars stick around forever."In the interview, which took place in New York, he said he would "encourage everybody" to let go of the past."If there's certain things from the past that are still affecting you every day, that's harder to let go of," he told GQ."But, for me, there's enough drama in the world and enough drama in people's lives to continue with issues with family."

schema.headline: Royals roll out the red carpet in Windsor for visiting Sultan

title: UK to deploy jets to defend Saudi Arabia from Houthi attacks
description: Figure caption, Watch: UK has 'responsibility to back allies and protect civilians', says defence secretaryUpdated 1 hour agoThe UK will deploy RAF Ty
body: Figure caption, Watch: UK has 'responsibility to back allies and protect civilians', says defence secretaryUpdated 1 hour agoThe UK will deploy RAF Typhoon jets to defend Saudi Arabia in response to escalating Houthi missile and drone attacks, the government has said.The defensive mission will help defend Saudi cities and infrastructure -  a move authorised by Prime Minister Andy Burnham - against aerial attacks by the Iran-backed group. It follows Houthi attacks on the Saudi capital Riyadh, as well as on energy sites on the country's coast. "These aircraft will operate in a defensive role and will not conduct offensive strikes against the Houthis," Defence Secretary Wes Streeting said in a written statement on Tuesday.Image source, MODImage caption, An RAF Typhoon in flight (file image)The Houthis are locked in a civil war with Yemen's internationally recognised government, which is backed by Saudi Arabia and were ousted by the group from capital, Sanaa, in 2014.Since September, Saudi Arabia has been struggling to defend its skies from Houthi attacks after a ceasefire of sorts in Yemen broke down.The Houthis launched a fresh offensive against Yemen's officially recognised government and seized effective control of the crucial Bab al Mandab strait.Government forces - backed by Saudi aircover - mounted a counter offensive and the Houthis in turn struck targets deep in Saudi territory.The Houthis successfully hit Saudi infrastructure including the King Khalid airport, energy facilities and key ports.Saudi authorities said last week that 19 people had been killed in Houthi attacks on the kingdom's airports. One missile strike on Riyadh's international airport on 10 October killed 13 people and injured 308 others – the deadliest attack in Saudi Arabia in more than a decade.Figure caption, Footage from inside Riyadh airport on 10 October shows the moment the strike hitHouthis have been retaliating for strikes on territory that they control in western Yemen, including the capital Sanaa.More than 70 security personnel were killed earlier this week in a Houthi missile strike on a camp in Yemen's central province of Shabwa.A spokesman for the Saudi-backed Yemeni armed forces said the Iran-backed group launched three ballistic missiles at al-Alam camp near Ataq city.The Houthis' military spokesman said they had targeted "Saudi enemy concentrations".According to the Houthi-run health ministry in north-western Yemen, Saudi air and artillery strikes have killed at least 141 people and injured 395 since 3 September.The government's health ministry, meanwhile, said last week that at least 1,282 people had been killed in the conflict across Yemen since 6 August.Saudi Arabia has struggled to bring down incoming missiles and drones because so much of its air defence capability was used up against Iranian attacks earlier this year. The sheer size of the country also makes it hard to provide comprehensive air defence.The UK warplanes will not only help Saudi Arabia defend its skies, but they will also free up the country's own aircraft to carry out offensives strikes against the Houthis.The UK will also deploy military advisers and an RAF A400M transport aircraft to support the movement of defence equipment within Saudi Arabia. It is already providing Saudi Arabia with defence support equipment to protect against aerial attacks and air-to-air refuelling for defensive Saudi operations. The refuelling has now been extended by 90 days. In a separate statement, Streeting said the targeting of Riyadh airport "shows the lengths the Houthis are going to escalate the situation in the region". "That's why today I have approved further UK military support," the defence secretary added. Streeting also pointed to violence in the Gulf disrupting energy supplies and increasing costs for families and businesses. Earlier this month, Houthi military spokesman Brig Gen Yahya Saree vowed to continue the "escalating operations deep inside Saudi Arabia".

schema.headline: UK to deploy jets to defend Saudi Arabia from Houthi attacks

title: Kim Jong Un: Why do rumours about his death keep coming back?
description: Kim Jong Un has appeared in North Korean state media looking remarkably healthy for a man rumoured to have died from a brain haemorrhage.Photographs p
body: Kim Jong Un has appeared in North Korean state media looking remarkably healthy for a man rumoured to have died from a brain haemorrhage.Photographs published by state newspaper Rodong Sinmun show the 42-year-old dictator touring what the paper said was a clothing and footwear exhibition with his daughter.The images emerged hours after a Chinese dissident who lives in the US claimed, without evidence, that Kim had been taken to a hospital in Beijing in a coma and had died.For those who watch North Korea closely, this kind of rumour has become almost routine.In one of the world's most secretive states, facts are often difficult to verify, creating fertile ground for speculation.This latest claim originated with Wanjun Xie, who identifies himself as chairman of the Chinese Democratic Party, a group banned by Chinese authorities. He has previously circulated unverified claims, including speculation about the death of Chinese leader Xi Jinping.Xie alleged that Kim suffered a severe brain haemorrhage and was transferred to Beijing because North Korea lacked the medical facilities to treat him. He claimed Kim later died and that his body had been secretly returned to North Korea, with the regime concealing his death.Yet the photographs tell a different story. Kim is seen examining displays, accompanied by Kim Ju Ae and his usual entourage of officials. While there is no way to know exactly when the images were taken, there are other reasons to doubt the claim.There would probably be signs beyond North Korea's borders if there were a sudden collapse in Kim's health.China could tighten security along its frontier to prepare for potential instability or refugee flows. Activity around North Korean diplomatic missions might also increase. Defectors in South Korea often receive information through informal networks along the Chinese border. None of this has happened. South Korean intelligence officials, meanwhile, told Yonhap they had heard nothing to support the reports.The rumour also echoes previous false alarms.In 2020, a high-profile North Korean defector claimed he was "99% certain" Kim had died following cardiovascular surgery. Not long afterwards, Kim appeared in public and the claim unravelled.So why do these rumours keep resurfacing? The first reason is succession.North Korea has been ruled by the Kim family for three generations, but what happens after Kim Jong Un remains less certain than it was for his predecessors.Kim Il Sung spent decades preparing his son, Kim Jong Il, for power. By the time Kim Il Sung died in 1994, the succession plan was firmly established. Kim Jong Il's transition was relatively smooth.Kim Jong Un's rise was faster and more precarious. After Kim Jong Il suffered a stroke in 2008, his youngest son was rapidly promoted through the ranks. By the time his father died in 2011, he had been publicly identified as the future leader. Even so, Kim Jong Un spent years consolidating power, purging rivals and eliminating perceived threats.Today, South Korea's intelligence agency believes he may be preparing his daughter as a successor. She has increasingly appeared at high-profile events and military displays.But she is thought to be only 13 years old. North Korea has never been led by a woman, and she has not been formally designated as heir. Her youth would also leave her vulnerable in any power struggle.All of this uncertainty helps explain why rumours about Kim's health attract so much attention.The second reason is that the rumours are not entirely implausible.Kim is overweight and a heavy smoker. South Korea's National Intelligence Service has repeatedly warned that his lifestyle puts him at higher risk of cardiovascular disease. Heart problems and strokes also run in the Kim family.If anything were to happen to Kim, the stakes are high for neighbouring countries and the wider international community. Any sudden leadership crisis raises difficult questions about control of North Korea's nuclear weapons and the prospect of political instability.Would a power struggle tempt hardliners to act aggressively? Could unrest trigger a refugee crisis along the Chinese border? These are questions that concern not only Beijing and Seoul but also Washington, which maintains around 28,000 troops in South Korea.Intelligence agencies watch Kim Jong Un closely so they are prepared for any news.Because North Korea remains an information black hole, it is also an easy target for false reports. Only a tiny circle has regular access to its leader. Even intelligence agencies struggle to obtain reliable information, and much of what emerges is heavily caveated as unverified or highly likely rather than confirmed fact.The regime itself is also suspected of deliberately encouraging confusion, leaking misleading information to obscure what is really happening inside the country.So it is hard to believe that Wanjun Xie had somehow stumbled across such significant news, when it had eluded those whose job it is to stay across it. He may simply have been seeking attention. Or he may have wanted to embarrass Beijing by highlighting its ties to Pyongyang, although those are well-established for the world to see.Whatever his motive, Xie is far from the first person to exploit the uncertainty surrounding North Korea's leadership.

schema.headline: Kim Jong Un: Why do rumours about his death keep coming back?

title: Cristiano Ronaldo let Manchester United down, says Erik ten Hag
description: Former Manchester United manager Erik ten Hag said Cristiano Ronaldo "let the team and let me down" during the Dutchman's spell at Old Trafford.Portug
body: Former Manchester United manager Erik ten Hag said Cristiano Ronaldo "let the team and let me down" during the Dutchman's spell at Old Trafford.Portugal forward Ronaldo was in his second spell at United when Ten Hag took charge in the summer of 2022 but left in controversial circumstances a few months later."He let the team down, and he let me down, because we planned with him," Ten Hag told The Athletic, external."I flew out to Portugal to speak with him about what I was aiming for before I came to United. "Obviously, he's one of the best in football history. I respected him a lot. But at that time, as a manager, I had to make a rational decision and keep the players I admire in."Ten Hag had dropped Ronaldo for a Premier League game at Chelsea in October 2022 after he had refused to come on as a substitute against Tottenham three days earlier.Ronaldo gave an interview in the November in which he said he felt "betrayed" by United, did not respect Ten Hag and was being forced out of the club prior to his departure being "mutually agreed".Ronaldo was 36 when he returned to Manchester United from Juventus in 2021, when Ole Gunnar Solskjaer was manager.Under Ten Hag, he scored just three goals in 16 outings before his exit during the 2022-23 campaign."It's the wrong idea to put this to me that I expected him to do the pressing, that he's exhausted," added Ten Hag. "But he couldn't. He ran neither in possession nor out of possession. The reason was because he didn't prepare himself."Every top team has to embrace the top player, but the top player has to work for the team."He was telling the players, 'save your legs at the training'. I understand it when you are top fit - you have sessions you can save the legs. But first you have to train yourself to get into the right fitness levels."The publication of Ten Hag's interview comes as Ronaldo has been given a 30-day suspension and fined 255 euros (£215) by the Portuguese Football Federation for leaving his country's international camp last month.Ten Hag was sacked by Manchester United in October 2024, having won the Carabao Cup in 2023 and FA Cup in 2024.On his time at Old Trafford, Ten Hag added he wanted to sign Frenkie de Jong, Harry Kane and Declan Rice, and was against the sale of Scott McTominay to Napoli in August 2024."I said for the first season, 'centre-half, there's a problem, centre-midfield, there is a problem, and especially I need a strategist, then we need goals'. And that was the biggest issue in all my three years: goals," said Ten Hag.

schema.headline: Cristiano Ronaldo let Manchester United down, says Erik ten Hag

title: Chancellor rejects calls to raise Capital Gains Tax in Budget
description: Chancellor John Healey has dismissed calls from some Labour MPs to increase Capital Gains Tax (CGT). Cabinet ministers Wes Streeting and Louise Haigh
body: Chancellor John Healey has dismissed calls from some Labour MPs to increase Capital Gains Tax (CGT). Cabinet ministers Wes Streeting and Louise Haigh both previously voiced support for raising CGT before Andy Burnham became prime minister in July. Ahead of next week's Budget, as first reported by the Times, external, Healey is minded not to increase CGT - which is imposed on the profit people make when they sell an asset that has increased in value, such as shares in a company or properties which are not primary residences.The move followed warnings that it could end up costing the government money if wealthy people leave the country or defer selling off assets.If you pay income tax at the basic rate then CGT is charged at 18%. For higher and additional rate income tax payers, the CGT rate is 24%.Last year, HMRC estimated, external that lifting the lower rate of CGT by 1% could raise £5m by 2028-9 but increasing the higher rate of CGT by 10% would reduce the Treasury's receipts by £3.6bn in 2028-9.The amount raised could be reduced if people adapt their behaviour to the tax rise, for example by moving abroad or deciding not to sell a property. The chancellor gave an indication of his approach last month in a speech when he spoke about the importance of businesses and self-employed people making profits."I want to see this country as a country of wealth creation. I want our government decisions and policies to raise the levels of confidence, and investment, and profit in British business," Healey said. Burnham has faced warnings against lifting CGT. His former adviser and Goldman Sachs Chief Economist Lord Jim O'Neill suggested it would send "the wrong message to business".But influential Labour figures had pushed for equalising CGT and income tax, with the former generally attracting a lower tax rate.Louise Haigh, a key ally of the prime minister, had suggested capital gains should go up to be closer to income tax, before she became Burnham's first secretary of state.In an article for the Renewal journal,, external Haigh argued that raising CGT would "shift the taxation burden away from punishing work, and towards unproductive capital accumulation which does little to grow the everyday economy". She said this could be accompanied by measures to ensure that "genuine investment returns are not penalised". Defence Secretary Wes Streeting called for a "wealth tax that works" in May, shortly after resigning as a minister in former Prime Minister Sir Keir Starmer's government.He had argued that equalising CGT with income tax would address an unfair system that was "penalising work".Healey had already ruled out levelling the two tax rates, according to a report in the Financial Times last week, external.Asked about the government's plans for CGT on BBC Breakfast, Communities Secretary Angela Rayner would not speculate on the Budget.Pressed over whether rejecting calls to increase the tax was a win for the rich, she said the government had already taken steps to give people "breathing space" and help with the cost of living.It comes after senior banking executives told the BBC they expect Healey to raise taxes on the sector. UK banks have been reporting bumper profits, leading to calls from unions for higher taxes.Healey is due to set out his tax and spending plans at his first Budget on 28 October, against the backdrop of the US-Iran war which has led to rising prices.The chancellor is under pressure to find measures to ease the cost of living and fund an increase for defence at his spending review next year. The chancellor's options for raising money are limited as Labour's 2024 manifesto pledged not to increase income tax, National Insurance and VAT, the three big revenue raisers. The government is also restricted in how much it can borrow due to its self-imposed rules on debt. In a pre-Budget speech on Tuesday, Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch urged the government to cut spending and reduce its borrowing.She said the prime minister and the chancellor should "live within our means" and pointed to her party's plan to save £70bn in cuts, including to welfare and overseas development aid. Badenoch told an audience in central London that Labour would not "find the courage" to cut spending. She said the chancellor wanted to deliver a "nothing to see here Budget" but added: "Britain cannot afford to do as little as possible."The Liberal Democrats have said the government could raise £14bn partly by introducing a windfall tax on the profits of banks.The party's deputy leader Daisy Cooper said the money could go towards cutting fuel duty, rail and bus fares and VAT for hospitality businesses.

schema.headline: Chancellor rejects calls to raise Capital Gains Tax in Budget

title: Marseille braces for more unrest after protests give way to 'apocalyptic' disorder
description: Figure caption, Watch: Clean up begins after some of the worst disorder in France's modern history, but police remainByNick BeakeEurope correspondentR
body: Figure caption, Watch: Clean up begins after some of the worst disorder in France's modern history, but police remainByNick BeakeEurope correspondentReporting fromMarseilleThunder and lightning have boomed across Marseille following the weekend's mayhem, illuminating the cracked windows and boarded-up doors of hundreds of businesses that were smashed as protests gave way to disorder.France's second city saw some of the worst violence as chaos gripped the country on Saturday. Local business leaders say more than 500 premises were damaged, and the majority looted.A police union boss told the BBC that the weekend had been an "apocalyptic" hell for his colleagues. 118 officers were injured, representing more than a tenth of the national figure.So far, 101 arrests have been made in the port city, a quarter of them children.But by Monday, it was police who were most conspicuous on the city's streets, not protesters. For eight hours, demonstrations and gatherings were banned in an effort to avoid a third consecutive day of disorder.It seemed to work; the largest central gathering we witnessed was a posse of weather-beaten tourists trudging around the quayside.Nonetheless, an overnight curfew for minors will come into force in parts of the city from Tuesday evening. An overnight curfew in parts of Paris, which came into force on Monday, has also been extended. Marseille is one of France's most ethnically diverse cities – a place where generations of new arrivals have landed.18-year-old student Maryame only arrived in the southern city a few weeks ago, albeit from the countryside not too far away."It was very scary because it's my first time in a big city, and also my first time demonstrating," she said.Image caption, Maryam (R) joined the protests on Saturday, which began in September over poor school conditions before escalating to cover broader issues such as the cost of livingMaryame said violence engulfed the student demonstration her friends had joined as looters began attacking shops.She said the solidarity of the earlier march was "beautiful" and the subsequent disorder "terrifying", but went on to say that she was conflicted as to whether even more violence would make the government sit up and listen."It is a very complicated question if violence is legitimate," she began."But the thing is, France, our history is really based on revolution, and sometimes we really have to make a really big impact."Sometimes it goes too far."'An unheard-of level of violence'For the police, the extent to which order disintegrated was a shock, according to one organisation representing rank and file officers."It was a war," said Arnaud Blaise from the UN1TE police union. "An unheard-of level of violence. Unprecedented."Looting was reported across the city centre, including along La Canebière - Marseille's equivalent of Paris's Champs-Élysées - Rue Paradis, and at the Centre Bourse shopping centre. Businesses were also hit further afield, such as in the Grand Littoral and Le Merlan shopping malls to the north.Image caption, Hundreds of businesses were looted in several locations across the cityBlaise said he was concerned that future protests could follow the same destructive pattern as Saturday, with young people from the deprived northern suburbs seizing the opportunity to steal amid chaos that, in his view, was stirred up by far-left agitators - referred to in France as the Black Bloc."The Black Blocs provoked, and the youngsters took advantage to start looting," Blaise said. "That created chaos, with police officers running right, running left, and in effect, we got overwhelmed."I put it to Blaise that the police had been accused of heavy-handedness with peaceful students but sitting back as the most violent protesters pillaged local businesses."That is not the case at all," he replied, arguing that more police than students had been injured."Four thousand tear gas grenades were fired and then we ran out of ammunition. So at a certain point, you have no choice but to retreat."France's Interior Minister Laurent Nuñez - whose resignation in the wake of the riots was rejected by President Macron - travelled to Marseille on Monday evening.He came to the City Hall, which was briefly occupied by protestors on Saturday, and met Marseille's Socialist Mayor Benoît Payan.Payan said he wanted answers from the government as to how the chaos was allowed to happen."Order was lost, and an attempt was made to restore order. I believe that from start to finish, it was a fiasco," he said on Monday.He said under-staffed and poorly deployed police needed to change their tactics."If there isn't a radical change of approach on this issue - if, by chance, the only target remains high school students - then we will see looting scenes again."He continued: "I don't know what's left to loot in Marseille, but for the little that remains, it will be looted."Image caption, Chantal Bellanger said she was worried for young people rioting out of anger and despairWhile the ban on public gatherings in Marseille and partial overnight curfews in other French cities have brought some temporary calm, more demonstrations are planned for the weekend.At a smashed out tram stop, 79-year-old grandmother Chantal Bellanger said she had been "worried - but then, I've been worried for a long time"."We can clearly see that France has lost its grip on many things. Public services, hospitals, education is in a horrible state, the peripheral neighbourhoods are dilapidated, they are abandoned."She said she used to work in these deprived northern suburbs, where poverty and crime rates are very high, and feared a whole lost generation was criminalising itself through anger and despair."It tugs at your heartstrings," she said."To see children whose actions are going to place them completely outside of society. It's painful to watch."Additional reporting by Paul Pradier and Pol Reygaerts

schema.headline: Marseille braces for more unrest after protests give way to 'apocalyptic' disorder

title: How is the US economy really doing under President Trump?
description: ByBen ChuPolicy and analysis correspondentPresident Donald Trump has been boasting about the performance of the US economy ahead of the midterm congre
body: ByBen ChuPolicy and analysis correspondentPresident Donald Trump has been boasting about the performance of the US economy ahead of the midterm congressional elections, claiming he has boosted incomes, reduced inflation and created jobs.Trump has repeatedly said: "We have the hottest country anywhere in the world."While the overall US economy is faring better than many expected after Trump launched his sweeping "Liberation Day" tariffs in 2025, there's evidence those import taxes and the impact of the US-Israel war with Iran have pushed up inflation, with the harmful effects felt by most American households.The US economy is also being helped by an AI investment boom, and could falter if that spending were to dry up.So how does all this feel for the average American? BBC Verify has looked at whether the evidence supports the president's claims. 1. US economy growingThe overall US economy is growing at a respectable clip by the country's recent historic standards.The latest data shows US GDP, external - which is how economists measure the size of the US economy - currently expanding at an annualised rate of 2.2%.And it has increased by around 3.2% overall since the end of 2024, just before Trump took office for his second term.That is more growth than any other member of the G7 group of leading economies over that period.The US growth rate has been faster than was forecast by the International Monetary Fund (IMF), external in the immediate wake of Trump's announcement of a swathe of new tariffs on goods coming into the US on 2 April 2025.It downgraded its forecasts at the time, citing the negative impact of Trump's import duties on investment and consumer spending.Though it is important to note that Trump eased the tariffs considerably in the months that followed, reducing the impact that had initially been expected on the economy.The US economy has also been heavily supported in recent years by American technology companies making massive investments in AI, including by constructing data centres around the country.Spending on building data centres, external (excluding the IT hardware to go in them) by US businesses in August 2026 was $5bn, almost double the monthly rate when Trump returned to office. 2. Inflation picked upMany American voters wanted to punish Joe Biden in the 2024 presidential election, holding him responsible for the pain caused by a significant spike in prices in the wake of the pandemic.The current rate of US inflation, external is 3.7%. That's still well down on the recent peak rate of 9% under Biden in 2022, but higher than the 3% rate that Donald Trump inherited in January 2025.Economists estimate, external US inflation would have been lower without the new tariffs imposed by Trump since he returned to office.While the impact of the Iran war on global energy prices, with the significant disruption to oil and fuel supplies from the Middle East, has also helped push up US domestic inflation.3. Household income growth held backAverage US household incomes are still rising under Trump.The median income - after adjusting for inflation - rose 2.6% in 2025 to $87,460, the highest on record, external.However, the Institute on Taxation and Economic Policy (ITEP) think tank has estimated the combined effects of the following, external on US households:- Trump's tax cuts- The expiry of extra government subsidies that had made health insurance cheaper for millions of Americans- Higher-than-expected price rises during Trump's second term, including those linked to tariffs and the Iran warITEP's conclusion is that the middle fifth of households are, on average, around $1,700 worse off in 2026 than they would have been, while the poorest fifth are around $750 worse off.The richest 1%, by contrast, are estimated to be an average of $12,560 better off than they woud have been, primarily because of Trump's tax cuts.ITEP's estimates about the impact of tariffs on American households of different income levels are broadly similar to those of the Tax Foundation think tank, external.4. Job creation slowed downTrump predicted his tariffs would result in America being "flooded with jobs", external as manufacturing firms set up new factories on US soil to avoid their products being taxed at the border.Since he returned to the White House, an average of 34,000 jobs have been added to the economy each month.​​But that is significantly down on the 122,000 jobs added each month in the final year of Biden's presidency, external.5. Borrowing costs risingThe growing deficit is also one of the reasons the US government gets charged more to borrow money in financial markets.The 10-year US government bond yield has risen sharply since Trump returned to office in January 2025 and is now above 5%, the highest rate since the global financial crisis in 2007.That increase in the market cost of US government borrowing also puts upward pressure on the interest rates on mortgages available to American households.The interest rate on a new 30-year US mortgage has risen to 7.4%, external per year, up from 6.9% when Trump returned to the White House.That's added to problems in the US housing market, making homes less affordable for new buyers. It has left many existing owners reluctant to move because doing so would mean giving up their cheaper mortgages, which they took out at lower rates, external and cannot take with them to a new property.Data graphics by Erwan Rivault.

schema.headline: How is the US economy really doing under President Trump?

title: Ronnie O'Sullivan: Why seven-time world champion faces a battle to stay in world's top 16
description: O'Sullivan has had a quiet start to the 2026-27 season, with a run to the semi-finals of the Wuhan Open the only significant result in his five tourna
body: O'Sullivan has had a quiet start to the 2026-27 season, with a run to the semi-finals of the Wuhan Open the only significant result in his five tournaments to date.Two last-16 finishes preceded his final-four finish at that event, but he has been defeated in the first round in his two subsequent appearances, in Shenzhen and Belfast.Having earned £513,750 at ranking events over two years, O'Sullivan is £99,350 ahead of Ali Carter, who holds 16th spot in the world rankings, and £154,650 clear of Zhou Yuelong, who sits in 17th, with winnings of £359,100.On first glance, that appears to be a comfortable cushion, with only a set of significant runs from his rivals putting him at risk of having to qualify for the World Championships in May next year.However, there are issues over the horizon, because over a third of O'Sullivan's winnings come from reaching the final of the Saudi Arabia Masters in August 2025.The £200,000 he won in Jeddah will continue to count towards his ranking past the 2027 World Championship, but that money will slip out of the eligibility period soon after the start of the 2027-28 season.O'Sullivan will also not be able to replace his earnings with another run at the event, after the tournament, which offered the highest prize money outside of UK-based competitions, was abolished in April.That means he is likely to need strong performances over the next 18 months to remain in contention for an automatic spot at the 2028 World Championship.O'Sullivan might improve his chances of earning ranking prize money by competing in more tournaments, having operated on a reduced schedule in recent years.It should be noted he has cited medical reasons or the need to prioritise his mental health for his withdrawals from several tournaments in recent years.He played predominantly in Asia in 2025-26, only competing in two tournaments in Britain - the UK Championship and World Championship.His appearance in Belfast this week was his first in a ranking event in the United Kingdom outside the Triple Crown events (Masters, World Championship, UK Championship) since the English Open in September 2024.His last ranking title came at the World Grand Prix in January of the same year.After his defeat in the semi-finals of the Wuhan Open in August, O'Sullivan said he did not "want to throw in the towel just yet".But he has also acknowledged he has limited time left in the sport, giving himself until 2028, external to beat Hendry's world title total by landing an eighth.Should he slip out of the top 16, O'Sullivan has said he has no interest in competing in World Championship qualifying - held this year at the English Institute of Sport in Sheffield - stating he would retire from snooker instead.There are 16 places available for the World Championship through the qualifying rounds, with Hendry, Mark Williams, Ding Junhui and Steve Davis among players past and present who have taken that route after slipping out of the elite 16 amid declining results.It seemingly holds no appeal to O'Sullivan, though."I'd love to win another World Championship. I've got two attempts at it," O'Sullivan told World Snooker Tour in July."If I don't do it this season or the next season, then it'll definitely never happen."I'm not going to play qualifiers. You won't be seeing me go down to Barnsley trying to win qualifying matches and all that sort of stuff."I have to be realistic. If that happens, then obviously that's the end of my career. But hopefully, I can keep going for at least another two seasons."Playing in more tournaments may be the most obvious way to avoid a difficult retirement decision, but O'Sullivan has spoken candidly about his battles with depression and anxiety and may feel he cannot compete more regularly.O'Sullivan has threatened to retire on multiple occasions during his career before deciding to stick with the sport, going back as far as his teenage years.Those have usually quickly been forgotten and the reality is that he has displayed remarkable longevity, with his first World Championship win coming in 2001 and his latest in 2022.However, faced with fading powers and a resulting lack of prize money, we may be entering the end stage of the all-time great's career.

schema.headline: Ronnie O'Sullivan: Why seven-time world champion faces a battle to stay in world's top 16

title: BBC Three, BBC Scotland and Radio 4 Extra channels to close
description: The BBC is to close its BBC Three and BBC Scotland television channels in the spring, as the corporation continues to make £500m of savings over two y
body: The BBC is to close its BBC Three and BBC Scotland television channels in the spring, as the corporation continues to make £500m of savings over two years.Both services will become online-only, meaning they will continue to produce and host some content on iPlayer, without the need to fill a terrestrial TV schedule.The BBC has also announced the closure of Radio 4 Extra, which largely airs speech programmes from the BBC's archive, including comedy, drama and documentaries.BBC director-general Matt Brittin said: "We need to make every pound work harder for audiences as we respond to the immediate cost pressures and reinvent the BBC for a changing world. We all know that means tough choices."Katie Razzall: Closures make business sense, but more savings are neededDiscussing the closure of linear broadcast services, Brittin said: "Much of the great content they currently carry will still be found where audiences already enjoy them on iPlayer and Sounds. "While this follows media speculation, I recognise the confirmation of this news will be hard for audiences and colleagues."Outlining the plans, the corporation confirmed:BBC Scotland will remain a channel on iPlayer, with some content also broadcast on BBC One and BBC Two in ScotlandBBC Three commissions, supported by increased investment in content for younger audiences, will be available on BBC iPlayer and on other platforms including YouTubeProgrammes from Radio 4 Extra will be available on BBC Sounds - while its religious programme The Daily Service will be on BBC Sounds and local radioBBC Three, which is aimed at young audiences and launched hits such as Fleabag and Gavin & Stacey, previously moved online in 2016, but was reinstated as a TV channel in 2022. BBC Scotland launched as a channel in 2019, broadcasting a variety of Scottish programming including news, sport, documentaries and entertainment.However, some of the shows that air on the two networks, such as Two Doors Down on BBC Scotland and Sort Your Life Out on BBC Three, are repeats of episodes originally broadcast on other more mainstream BBC channels.Both networks currently only broadcast TV programming in the evenings, although BBC Scotland simulcasts BBC Radio Scotland during the rest of the day.The BBC said that the network's nightly programme Reporting Scotland: News at Seven will not move to BBC iPlayer and will cease when the linear channel closes. Audiences will continue to be served by BBC Scotland's wider news offering, including Reporting Scotland, The Sunday Show, Radio Scotland Breakfast, Debate Night and Scotcast, the corporation said.  While Radio 4 Extra does air some original programming, its schedule is predominantly made up of archive content, much of which is available on BBC Sounds.Entertainment trade union Equity said Tuesday's announcement "does not signal a thriving BBC, and we are concerned about the UK's preeminent public service broadcaster's ability to meet its duties to the fullest".Affected staff were told about the changes on Tuesday, although the proposed closure of BBC Scotland and BBC Three had been reported by some media outlets in recent weeks.The BBC is aiming to cut between 1,800 and 2,000 jobs - almost one in 10 - in an attempt to save £500m over two years as it faces "significant financial pressures".Around 550 job closures have already been announced in news, while more than 30 job cuts have so far been announced for BBC Sport.The newly appointed director of BBC News, Rachel Jupp, announced on Tuesday that a further £5.5m of savings were being proposed, which would represent the closure of around 100 roles. Meanwhile, several high-profile BBC TV series have been cancelled altogether in recent weeks. RuPaul's Drag Race UK, Blankety Blank, Celebrity Mastermind, Live at the Apollo, Football Focus and Ski Sunday are among the programmes the BBC has dropped so far, while other formats such as DIY SOS have been temporarily rested.

schema.headline: BBC Three, BBC Scotland and Radio 4 Extra channels to close
